stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: The words for library, office and desk all share the three letters k-t-b. What do you think they have in common?
explain: Vocabulary grows fast in Arabic because words come from roots. The root k-t-b (writing) gives kitāb (book), kātib (writer), maktaba (library) and maktab (office or desk). The prefix ma- often makes a place: madrasa (school, from d-r-s, "study"), maṭbakh (kitchen).

City words: mustashfā (hospital), maṭʿam (restaurant), sūq (market), jāmiʿa (university), maṭār (airport), ṭabīb (doctor), ṣadīq (friend). Learn them with their roots when you can, so you can guess new words.
From level 3 the words are shown with fewer vowel marks, as in real texts. Say them aloud with the short vowels you learned before.
stages.mnemonic: Ma- is a map-maker: it marks the place where the action happens.
sentences: The library is near the university.
My friend works in a hospital.
We eat at the restaurant today.

gq.q: Which word shares the root k-t-b (writing) with kitāb?
gq.why: Maktaba comes from k-t-b. The others come from other roots.

gq.q: What does the prefix ma- often add to a root?
gq.why: Ma- + root often names the place of an action: maktab, madrasa, maṭʿam.

panel.q: A learner knows that ṭaʿām means food. What is maṭʿam most likely?
o: A place for food, a restaurant
A kind of fruit or a food dish
panel.why: The ma- place pattern on ṭ-ʿ-m gives a place of food.

panel.q: Why is it helpful to learn Arabic words with their roots?
o: One root gives several related words, so you can guess new words
Roots tell you how to spell English words that come from Arabic
Roots show which words are borrowed
panel.why: Words from one root share a core meaning.

panel.q: Explain how the root idea helps you guess the meaning of maktab if you know kitāb and kātib.
panel.model: They share the root k-t-b (writing). Ma- makes a place noun, so maktab is a place where writing happens: an office or a desk.
panel.why: Root plus pattern gives a predictable meaning.

teach.model: Many Arabic words grow from a three-letter root. The prefix ma- often marks a place, like maktab and maktaba from the root k-t-b for writing.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: "I will not go" and "I did not go" use different little words in Arabic. Why might Arabic need three different "not" words?
explain: Arabic has three main tenses in speech: past (kataba), present (yaktubu) and future (sa-yaktubu or sawfa yaktubu). The future is made by sa- or sawfa before the present verb.

Negation depends on time. Present: lā + present (lā aktubu, I do not write). Past: lam + short present (lam aktub, I did not write). Future: lan + present (lan aktuba, I will not write). The verb after lam and lan changes its ending slightly.
Time words: dāʾiman (always), aḥyānan (sometimes), ghāliban (often), al-ān (now), qarīban (soon), qabla (before), baʿda (after). Time words usually go near the verb or at the end of the sentence.
stages.mnemonic: Lā = now, lam = then, lan = later: L, L, L for Not now, Not then, Not later.

gq.q: Which word negates a past event, as in "he did not go"?
gq.why: Lam + the short present verb gives a past negative.

gq.q: What do the prefixes sa- or sawfa show?
gq.why: Sa- or sawfa + present verb = future.

panel.q: Why is "lan" the right negator in "I will not go tomorrow"?
o: Lan is only used with nouns
panel.why: Lan + present verb is the standard future negative.

panel.q: A learner writes "lā dhahabtu" for "I did not go". What is the correct form?
panel.why: For past negation use lam + the short present: lam adhhab. Lam is not used with the past verb form.

panel.q: Name the three negative words for present, past and future and say which time each belongs to.
panel.model: Lā negates the present, lam the past and lan the future.
panel.why: Arabic chooses the negative word by time.

teach.model: Arabic marks the future with sa- or sawfa. To say not, use lā for now, lam for the past and lan for the future.

points.ask: How do I show the future?
How does negation depend on time?

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: "I stayed home because it rained." One word links the two ideas. What kind of word is it?
explain: Longer sentences are built with connectors: li-anna (because), lākin (but), idhā (if), ʿindamā (when), thumma (then), ḥattā (until), anna (that), wa (and). The word anna (that) is followed by a noun or pronoun in the accusative.

A relative clause uses alladhī (who or which, masculine) and allatī (feminine). It agrees with the thing it describes in gender and number: al-kitāb alladhī qaraʾtuhu, "the book that I read". Notice the extra "-hu" (it) pointing back to the book. Arabic repeats the object pronoun in this kind of clause.
Writers often join clauses with wa, "and", and many sentences follow each other in a flowing line. Speakers of dialect may use different connectors, but the MSA ones are understood everywhere.
stages.mnemonic: Alladhī carries the noun back: "the book THAT I read IT".
sentences: I stayed home because the weather is rainy.
The book that I read is long.
If you study well, you will succeed.

gq.q: Which word is used for "who/which" with a feminine noun?
gq.why: Allatī is the feminine relative; alladhī is masculine.

gq.q: In "al-kitāb alladhī qaraʾtuhu", what does the final -hu mean?
o: his book (it shows who owns the book)
gq.why: The pronoun -hu points back to the book in the relative clause.

panel.q: Why is "al-bint allatī zurtuhā" correct for "the girl whom I visited"?
o: allatī matches the feminine noun and -hā points back to her
alladhī is always used, since it never changes for gender
panel.why: Relative pronouns and the returning pronoun agree with the noun.

panel.q: Which sentence is conditional?
panel.why: Idhā begins the condition.

panel.q: Why do learners need to add -hu in a relative clause such as "the book that I read"?
panel.model: Arabic repeats the object as a pronoun inside the clause (qaraʾtuhu, "I read it"), referring back to the book.
panel.why: English leaves the object out; Arabic keeps a returning pronoun.

teach.model: Use li-anna for because, lākin for but and idhā for if. Use alladhī for who or which and add a pronoun that points back to the noun.

points.ask: How do I say the book that I read?
What is the extra pronoun for?

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: Many stories start with "Once upon a time". How might an Arabic storyteller begin?
explain: Arabic stories often begin with dhāta yawm (one day, "on a day") or kāna yā mā kāna (a Levantine fairy-tale opening, "there was and there was not"). Folk tales feature characters such as the clever and funny Juḥā, who appears in many countries.

The most famous story collection is The Thousand and One Nights (Alf layla wa layla). A frame story tells of Shahrazad, who tells stories every night to the king so that she can live. The tales gather material from Persia, India and Arab lands.
When you read a story, look at the verbs first. Past tense often tells what happened, while the present can give vivid action. Find the characters, the place, the problem and the end (an-nihāya).
stages.mnemonic: Story = who, where, problem, end: four questions for any tale.
sentences: One day there was a wise king.
The boy found a small key.
In the end the king laughed.

gq.q: Who tells stories to the king in The Thousand and One Nights?
gq.why: Shahrazad tells a tale each night to keep the king from ending her life.

gq.q: Which Arabic phrase is a common story opening?

panel.q: Why is the frame story of the Nights a clever literary idea?
o: It lets many separate tales sit inside one story
It means the book has only one tale
It means the book has only one tale told in many ways
panel.why: A frame story holds other stories inside it.

panel.q: In "wajada al-walad miftāḥan", what does the verb tell you?
o: The boy found something in the past
The boy is finding something now
The boy is finding something right now
panel.why: Wajada is a past-tense verb.

panel.q: Name one thing to look for when you read a short story in Arabic.
panel.model: Look for the characters, the setting and the problem and how it ends.
panel.why: Story elements guide comprehension.

teach.model: Many stories start with dhāta yawm, one day. Look for characters, place, problem and ending. The Thousand and One Nights is a famous collection with the storyteller Shahrazad.

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: Say "kalb" (dog) and "qalb" (heart). The only difference is one sound at the start. Can a listener hear it?
explain: Some Arabic sounds sit close together, so careful listening matters. ك (k) is soft and ق (q) is deep: kalb means dog, qalb means heart. س (s) and ص (ṣ) differ: sayf (sword) and ṣayf (summer). Ṣ is "emphatic", said with a heavier tongue.
Also listen for the throat sounds ʿ (ع) and ḥ (ح), and for length: ʿilm (knowledge) and ʿalam (flag) differ by vowels. In Arabic, vowel length changes meaning, so train your ear.
When you listen to Arabic in the news, you hear MSA. In films and songs you often hear a dialect, such as Egyptian or Levantine. Listen first for the topic and the question words, then for details.
stages.mnemonic: Heavy letter, heavy mouth: ص ض ط ظ make nearby vowels deeper.
sentences: Summer is hot in the desert.
The flag is on the building.
Knowledge in youth is like engraving on stone.

gq.q: What is the difference between kalb and qalb?
o: The first sound: k (dog) and q (heart)
The vowel length in the middle of the word
gq.why: The deep q changes the meaning.
ص (ṣ), ض, ط and ظ are the emphatic letters.

panel.q: A listener hears "seef" instead of "ṣayf" and understands "sword" instead of "summer". What is the cause?
o: The emphatic ص was pronounced as the plain س
The word was said in a dialect, not in MSA
The speaker used the wrong tense
panel.why: Mixing س and ص changes the word.

panel.q: Why is it important to hear the vowels in ʿilm and ʿalam?
o: The vowels differ and so do the meanings
Length never matters in Arabic, only the consonants do
panel.why: Different vowels make different words.

panel.q: Name two pairs of sounds that learners confuse in Arabic.
panel.model: For example k and q (kalb/qalb), and s and ṣ (sayf/ṣayf).
panel.why: Close pairs are a common listening challenge.

teach.model: Some Arabic sounds are very close, such as k and q, or s and ṣ. A small change can give a new word. Vowel length matters too.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: You need to interrupt politely, agree or ask for time. Which small phrases make a conversation smooth?
explain: Conversation phrases: law samaḥta (excuse me, please, to a man), bi-ṭ-ṭabʿ (of course), lā mushkila (no problem), uwāfiq (I agree), aẓunnu anna (I think that), ḥaqqan? (really?), rubbamā (maybe), intaẓir laḥẓa (wait a moment).
Pronunciation hints: pronounce the throat sounds ʿ and ḥ clearly; do not shorten long vowels; say a doubled letter with a short pause. Stress usually falls on the long or heavy syllable.

Address people politely with yā + name: yā Aḥmad, yā ustādh. Use the polite forms you learned: -ka for a man, -ki for a woman. In dialects, phrases change: "of course" is ṭabʿan in Egypt and Levant, bi-ṭ-ṭabʿ in MSA.
stages.mnemonic: Law samaḥta opens a door; laḥẓa buys a moment.
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?
I think the idea is good.
Maybe we will meet at five.

gq.q: How do you address a man named Ahmad when calling to him?
gq.why: Yā + name is the calling form.

panel.q: A learner says "lā mushkila" when the shopkeeper asks if it is fine to wait. What does this convey?
o: There is no problem: I am happy to wait
There is a big problem and I will not wait
panel.why: Lā mushkila is a casual reassurance.

panel.q: Why is it polite to start a question with "law samaḥta"?
o: It softens the request, like "excuse me"
It means "stop" and tells the listener to be quiet
panel.why: The phrase is a courtesy opener.

panel.q: Give one way to show disagreement politely in Arabic.
panel.model: You can say "lā uwāfiq" (I do not agree) and soften it with "rubbamā" or "lākin", or give your opinion with "aẓunnu anna".
panel.why: Softeners keep disagreement polite.

teach.model: Use law samaḥta to excuse yourself, uwāfiq to agree and rubbamā for maybe. Say aẓunnu anna to give an opinion. Pronounce long vowels and throat sounds clearly.

points.ask: How do I get someone's attention politely?
How do I agree or give an opinion?
What should I watch in pronunciation?

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: A good paragraph guides the reader: first, next, finally. Which little words in Arabic do that job?
explain: Paragraph linkers in Arabic: awwalan (first), thāniyan (second), thumma (then), aydan (also), lākin (but), li-dhālika (therefore), mathalan (for example), fī l-khitām (in conclusion).

An Arabic paragraph often starts with a main idea, adds support with examples, and closes with a summary. Arabic writing likes long, flowing sentences joined by wa, but for school writing you should vary sentence length.
Check each sentence: Does the adjective agree with its noun? Is the verb in the right tense? Do the connectors show how ideas relate? Add punctuation: the comma is ، and the question mark is ؟.
stages.mnemonic: First, Then, Finally: awwalan, thumma, fī l-khitām.
sentences: First I wake up, then I study.
I like summer, but winter is cold.

gq.why: Li-dhālika links a result to a cause.

gq.q: What is the Arabic comma symbol?
gq.why: The Arabic comma is ، and ؟ is the question mark.

panel.q: Why do writers add "mathalan" in a paragraph?
o: To introduce an example that supports the main idea
To end the paragraph and sum up the argument
panel.why: It means "for example".

panel.q: A student writes five sentences all joined with wa. What is a good revision?
o: Use connectors like lākin and li-dhālika and split some sentences
panel.why: Variety of connectors shows relationships.

panel.q: Name two features of a good paragraph.
panel.model: It has a clear main idea, supporting examples and a closing sentence.
panel.why: A paragraph is organised around a main point.

teach.model: Start with a main idea, add examples with mathalan and join ideas with words like lākin and li-dhālika. End with fī l-khitām.

points.ask: How do I begin a paragraph?
How do I support the idea?

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: Before eating many Arabic speakers say "bismillāh". What do you say in your language before a meal?
explain: Many everyday Arabic phrases involve God's name and are used by speakers of different religions as part of the culture. Examples: in shāʾ Allāh (God willing), mā shāʾ Allāh (admiration), al-ḥamdu lillāh (thank God), bismillāh (before starting), jazāk Allāhu khayran (may God reward you).

Festive greetings: ʿīd mubārak (blessed festival) and kull ʿām wa-antum bi-khayr (may every year find you well). Proverbs are valued: "al-waqtu ka-s-sayf" says that time cuts like a sword if you waste it.
Idioms can be tricky: ʿalā ʿaynī wa-raʾsī means "on my eye and head", i.e. gladly, with pleasure. A literal translation would confuse. Always ask for the meaning in context.
stages.mnemonic: Idioms are gifts: open them, do not just read the wrapping.
items: in the name of God (before starting)
with pleasure (lit. "on my eye and head")
may you be well every year
sentences: Time is like a sword: if you do not cut it, it cuts you.
Eid Mubarak to you and your family.
May God reward you well, my friend.

gq.q: When do people say mā shāʾ Allāh?
o: To express admiration, for example of a child or a gift
To say goodbye to a guest at the door
gq.why: It expresses admiration and good will.

gq.q: What does "ʿalā ʿaynī wa-raʾsī" mean idiomatically?
o: My eye hurts and my head too
gq.why: It is a warm way to accept a request.

panel.q: Why would a literal translation of "ʿalā ʿaynī wa-raʾsī" mislead a learner?
o: Its meaning is figurative and cannot be understood from the words
It is a rude expression that people should avoid saying
panel.why: Idioms need contextual translation.

panel.q: Why are these religious phrases used even by speakers of different religions?
o: They are part of everyday culture and language
They are compulsory in law for every speaker of Arabic
panel.why: Over time they became general social formulas.

panel.q: What does the proverb "al-waqtu ka-s-sayf" teach?
panel.model: Time is like a sword: if you do not use it wisely it will cut you; time is precious.
panel.why: The proverb compares time to a sword to warn against wasting it.

teach.model: Phrases like in shāʾ Allāh, mā shāʾ Allāh and bismillāh are common in daily life. Idioms must be understood by meaning, not word by word.

points.ask: How do I understand an idiom?

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: At an airport in Cairo, Beirut or Riyadh, the signs are in Arabic and English. Which Arabic words would you like to know first?
explain: Travel words: maṭār (airport), jawāz safar (passport), tadhkira (ticket), funduq (hotel), maḥaṭṭa (station), kharīṭa (map), yamīn (right), yasār (left), mubāsharatan (straight on). Learn them with min faḍlik: min faḍlik, ayna al-maḥaṭṭa?
A reservation is ḥajz. A common phrase is ʿindī ḥajz fī l-funduq, "I have a reservation at the hotel". For directions: inʿaṭif yamīnan thumma sir mubāsharatan, "turn right, then go straight".

Dialects differ in daily words. "Now" is al-ān in MSA, dilwaʾtī in Egyptian, halʾ in Levantine and al-ḥīn in Gulf Arabic. Learn the MSA words first, then pick up the local ones from the people you meet.
sentences: I have a reservation at the hotel.
Where can I buy a ticket?

gq.q: Which word is "now" in Egyptian Arabic?
gq.why: Dilwaʾtī is Egyptian; al-ān is MSA; halʾ is Levantine; al-ḥīn is Gulf.

gq.q: What does "inʿaṭif yamīnan" tell you to do?

panel.q: Why can a traveller mix MSA and dialect safely?
o: MSA is understood widely, while dialect words help locally
Dialects are illegal in writing, so only MSA may be spoken
panel.why: MSA works as the common base; dialect words add local flavour.

panel.q: On a sign you see "maḥaṭṭat al-qiṭār". What does it most likely say?
panel.why: Qiṭār is train; maḥaṭṭa is station.

panel.q: How would you ask politely where the station is?
panel.model: Law samaḥta, ayna al-maḥaṭṭa? (Excuse me, where is the station?)
panel.why: Polite opener plus ayna plus the place.

teach.model: Say law samaḥta, then ayna and the place. Know the words for ticket, hotel, right and left. Dialects differ, but MSA is widely understood.

points.ask: How do I ask where something is?
